Written Exam

Exam consisting of 8 learning test sections assessing knowledge and understanding of the
Organization Theory and Design topics.
Each section, not more than 25 minutes, will be independently graded
Threshold to pass is 18/30 an maximum Mark is 30/30.
The final mark is obtained as the average of marks given to each section of the written
exam: 0,25 rounded to the superior number
Each Test consists of 30 multiple choice questions with 4 possible alternatives.
Each correct answer adds 1 point, for each wrong answer you take off a point, if you do
not answer the score remains unchanged.
In some Tests some questions are replaced by twice as many statements that require you
to indicate as a true/false answer. For true/false answers you add or subtract 0.5.
Example of questions will be available for each Learning Test.

Sections of Learning Test are:
LEARNING TEST 1: Chapter 1 and 2
LEARNING TEST 2: Chapter 3
LEARNING TEST 3: Chapter 4, 5 and 6
LEARNING TEST 4: Chapter 7
LEARNING TEST 5: Chapter 8
LEARNING TEST 6: Chapter 9 and 10
LEARNING TEST 7: Chapter 11
LEARNING TEST 8: Chapter 12 and 13
There is the possibility to take the learning tests, 2 at a time, after the related topics have
been completed, during the course of Organization Theory and Design during the lessons.

Calculus – Part 2

Prof. Luca Rondi

Programme — academic year 2023/2024

Integration of functions of one variable.
Definite integrals and method of exhaustion. Definition of integrable functions and
classes of integrable functions: integrability of monotone functions and of continuous
functions. Properties of the definite integrals: monotonicity, mean theorem, integra-
bility of the sum, product, absolute value of integrable functions, additivity with
respect to the integration domain. Integrability of functions with a finite number of
discontinuities. Indefinite integrals. Fundamental theorem of integral calculus. Inte-
gration methods: integration by parts and by substitution. Integration of rational
functions.

Topology in Euclidean spaces.
Definition of distance. Definition of neighbourhoods, open sets, closed sets. Definition
of the interior, closure and boundary of a set. Definition of adherent, accumulation
and isolated points. Properties and characterizations of closed and open sets.

Differential calculus in several variables.
Partial derivatives and directional derivatives. Differentiable functions. Jacobian ma-
trix and gradient. Tangent space to the graph. Continuity of partial derivatives im-
plies differentiability. Differential of the composition of maps (chain rule). Mean
value theorem and its consequences. Higher order derivatives and Hessian matrix.
Taylor formula of order 2.

Maximum and minimum problems.
Necessary and sufficient conditions for local maxima and minima. Implicit func-
tion theorem. Geometric properties of the gradient and of level sets. Constrained
minimum problems. Lagrange multiplier theorem.

Multiple integrals. Definition of Riemann integral in several variables. Peano-
Jordan measure: measurable sets and sets of measure 0. Properties of the integral
and of the measure. Reduction theorem and applications: integration on normal
regions in the plane; integration by lines and by planes in the space. Change of
variables: polar coordinates in the plane and spherical and cylindrical coordinates
in the space. Guldino theorem.

Ordinary differential equations. Definition of Cauchy problem and examples.
First order linear equations. Equations with separable variables. Second order ho-
mogeneous linear equations with constant coefficients.

             Is “wc” a Natural Language Processing application?

 ●   In other words: what is the difference between data processing and
     language processing?
 ●   Bytes and lines are data, but words are linguistic objects

               Knowledge of language makes the difference

1. Given the following table that contains words (rows) and contexts (columns)
   co-occurrences:

   and the following sentences:
   ● The dog is a loyal and friendly mammal that many people choose as a pet
   ● My cat loves to play with its toys and is a wonderful pet to have around the house
   ● The colorful bird chirped melodiously showcasing its beautiful feathered plumage
   ● In the backyard we have a pond where a vibrant orange fish gracefully swims among
     aquatic plants
   ● Despite being a small bird the canary has striking feathered colors and a delightful
     song
   First, update the previous table (without adding new words and context
   words) including the occurrences in the provided sentences using a context
   window of 5.
   Provide the definition of PPMI (including the formula), and compute the
   weight assigned to at least two pairs (word, context) of the terms in the
   table. What are the solutions for handling rare words with PPMI? Why do
   we need them?

2. Given the following reference and translations provided by systems A and B

   Reference: A cat is on the table .
   System A: A pen is on the mat .
   System B: The cat was on a desk .

   Provide the definition of BLEU score and calculate its value (BLEU up to
   4-gram) for both translations. Additionally, what are adequacy and fluency
   in the context of machine translations? What are the problems with human
   evaluation in the context of machine translations?

3. What is an n-gram language model, and how does it work? How is the
   probability of a sentence computed? Discuss the challenges posed by data
   sparsity in n-gram language models and how to address them.

4. What do we intend for positional encoding in a Transformer model and why
   has it been introduced? What are the criteria that should be satisfied for
   building a positional encoding mechanism?

5. What is meant by the Sparsity challenge in NLP? Please elaborate on this
   concept.

Productory in i of P(yi|y1,..yi-1, x)

complete sentences

1    Goal
Develop a search engine that retrieves and ranks medical literature in response to precision medicine information needs
for oncology cases. Each search query corresponds to a synthetic patient case describing cancer type, genetic variants,
demographic details, and other relevant clinical factors. The system should be capable of identifying and ranking clin-
ical trials that discuss effective treatments for the given molecular and clinical profile. It must address challenges such
as interpreting structured and semi-structured medical information, understanding genomic and clinical terminology,
matching relevant treatments and variants.
    For the purpose of this project, we will focus exclusively on retrieving clinical trials addressing relevant treatments
for the given patient. This corresponds to the TREC 2019 Precision Medicine clinical trials subtask.

2    Project Description and Material
This project enables students to explore and apply approaches that combine Information Retrieval and Natural
Language Processing techniques in practice. Students can leverage knowledge acquired from previous courses, material
presented during this course, and external resources to develop their own ideas.
The project aims to help students gain a solid understanding of medical Information Retrieval systems and the specific
challenges of representing domain-specific (i.e. medical language). To aid the students, dedicated resources will be
provided. Students are expected to analyze the provided document collection, conduct baseline experiments using the
lab materials, and then design and implement their own approach to address the task of medical literature retrieval
through clinical trials. Finally, students will effectively communicate their investigation by clearly presenting their
methodology, findings, and insights in both a written report and an oral presentation.

face. They are encouraged to explore the dataset by analyzing term distributions, entity (e.g. disease, treatments)

1. A Document Collection: A static set of documents (the corpus) to be searched.

2. A Set of Topics (Queries): A set of formal descriptions of information needs (often including a title,
               description, and narrative) that represent what a user might search for.

3. Relevance Judgments (Ground Truth): A binary or graded list indicating which documents are
               relevant to which topics.
           These components are typically created through a rigorous process, such as those used by TREC (Text
           REtrieval Conference). First, documents are crawled or gathered to form the corpus. Then, domain
           experts or organizers formulate the queries. Crucially, the relevance judgments are created by human
           assessors. Since it is impossible to judge millions of documents for every query, a technique called
           Pooling is often used: the top k results from various different search systems are merged into a "pool,"
           and only these documents are judged by humans. Any document not in the pool is assumed to be
           irrelevant.
           Regarding the second part of the question, Precision@1 (P@1) is the preferred metric for Navigational
           Queries (or Known-Item Search). A classic example is a user searching for "Facebook login" or asking a
           digital assistant (like Siri) "What is the capital of Italy?". In these specific tasks, the user has a single,
           correct destination in mind or requires one specific fact. The user experience is binary: if the first result is
           correct, the system succeeds; if the user has to scroll to the second result, the system has failed to
           provide the instant access expected. Therefore, measuring how often the very first item is relevant is the
           only metric that truly reflects user satisfaction in this context.

1. Initialization: A random selection of observations from the dataset is made to serve as
   the initial centroids for the current iteration.

2. Assignment: Each observation is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is most similar
(closest in distance) to the observation itself.

3. Convergence Check: If no observations are reassigned to a different cluster compared to
the previous step, the algorithm terminates, having reached convergence.

4. Update and Iteration: Otherwise, a new centroid is calculated for each cluster as the
mathematical average of all observations currently belonging to it. The process then
returns to Step 2.

This algorithm is highly sensitive to outliers, which can significantly skew the average
values and displace centroids from their optimal positions. Conducting a thorough data
cleaning process beforehand is strongly recommended.

 After the three-valued logics: generalizations to n-valued logics for
 arbitrary number of truth values n ≥ 2.
 In the 1930s, various n-valued logics were developed.
 Usually truth values are assigned by rational number in [0, 1].
 Key idea: uniformly divide [0, 1] into n truth values.

 Definition

 0 1 2 n−2 n−1
 * +

 n−1 n−1 n−1 n−1 n−1

 Primitives in n-valued Logics
 Łukasiewicz proposed first series of n-valued logics for n ≥ 2.
 In the early 1930s, he simply generalized his three-valued logic.
 It uses truth values in Tn and defines primitives as follows:

 ¬a = 1 − a
 a ∧ b = min(a, b) a → b = min(1, 1 + b − a)
 a ∨ b = max(a, b) a ↔ b = 1 − |a − b|
 + another pair of and/or

 The n-valued logic of Łukasiewicz is denoted by Ln .
 The sequence (L2 , L3 , . . . , L∞ ) contains the classical two-valued logic
 L2 and an infinite-valued logic L∞ (rational countable values T∞ ).
 The infinite-valued logic L1 (standard Łukasiewicz logic) is the logic
 with all real numbers in [0, 1] (1 = cardinality of continuum).

 Semantics of Fuzzy Sets
 What membership grades may mean?

 Fuzzy sets are relevant in three types of information-driven tasks:
 classification and data analysis,
 decision-making problems,
 approximate reasoning.

 These three tasks exploit three semantics of membership grades:
 similarity
 preference
 possibility

R. Kruse, C. Doell FS – Fuzzy Sets and Fuzzy Logic Part 1 24 / 119

 Degree of Similarity

 Oldest interpretation of membership grades.
 µ(u) is degree of proximity of u from prototype elements of µ.
 Goes back to interests of fuzzy set concept in pattern classification.
 Still used today for cluster analysis, regression, etc.
 Here, proximity between pieces of information is modelled.
 Also, in fuzzy control: similarity degrees are measured between current
 situation and prototypical ones.

R. Kruse, C. Doell FS – Fuzzy Sets and Fuzzy Logic Part 1 25 / 119

 Degree of Possibility

 This interpretation was implicitly proposed by Zadeh when he
 introduced possibility theory and developed his theory of approximate
 reasoning.

 µ(u) can be viewed as:
 • degree of possibility that parameter X has value u
 • given the only information “X is µ”.

 Then support values are mutually exclusive and membership degrees
 rank these values by their possibility.

R. Kruse, C. Doell FS – Fuzzy Sets and Fuzzy Logic Part 1 27 / 119

 Degree of Preference

 µ represents both:
 • set of more or less preferred objects and
 • values of a decision variable X .
 µ(u) represents both:
 • intensity of preference in favor of object u and
 • feasibility of selecting u as value of X .
 Fuzzy sets then represent criteria or flexible constraints.

 This has been used in
 • fuzzy optimization (especially fuzzy linear programming) and
 • decision analysis.
 Typical applications: engineering design and scheduling problems.

Exercise 1. Write the fitness function for a genetic algorithm aimed at solving the Sudoku puzzle.
A Sudoku puzzle consists of a 9x9 grid, in which each cell must contain a number between 1 and 9,
according to the following rules:
 • Each row must contain exactly one instance of each number (no repetitions on rows)
 • Each column must contain exactly one instance of each number (no repetitions on columns)
 • The grid is divided in 9 3x3 sub-grids: each sub-grid must contain exactly one instance of
 each number (no repetitions on sub-grids)
You can assume that the input to the function is given in the form of a matrix indexed as:
 individual[row][column]
in which each cell contains a number between 1 and 9.

problem. In the Knapsack problem you are tasked with the goal of filling a knapsack (having
maximum capacity) with items from a list, maximizing the total value of the knapsack but without
exceeding the capacity. There is a single copy of each item and each item has a weight and value.
You can assume that the input to the function is given in the form of:
